tldr: This study introduces Autoregressive Normalizing Flows (AR-NFs), which enable exact likelihood computation, into offline reinforcement learning for robotic manipulation. By combining a sampling-free RL algorithm during training with one-step distillation at inference time, it achieves both strong task performance and an ~8.5x speedup.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of RoMAN-Flow. It maps continuous action chunks to latent variables reversibly conditioned on multimodal inputs. In offline reinforcement learning (NF-IQL), it directly maximizes the advantage-weighted likelihood of actions in the dataset. At inference time, actions are generated through the inverse transformation from latent variables.
overview:
In robotic manipulation, widely used approaches like Diffusion Policy and Flow Matching can express complex action distributions, but they cannot easily compute exact action log-likelihoods (the probability density of choosing an action). As a result, it has been difficult to apply "offline reinforcement learning that directly increases likelihoods," a paradigm that has been remarkably successful in language models. While autoregressive models with discrete tokenization can evaluate likelihoods, quantization errors often degrade the smooth, fine-grained continuous control required for robotics.

To tackle this, the authors turned to Autoregressive Normalizing Flows (AR-NFs), which have developed rapidly in image generation. AR-NFs offer ideal properties: high expressiveness in continuous action spaces and fast, exact likelihood evaluation via invertible transformations. However, AR-NFs suffer from a major bottleneck: sequential sampling (inverse transformation) is slow, making both sampling during training and low-latency inference on physical robots difficult.

RoMAN-Flow was proposed to solve this issue. In the reinforcement learning phase, it adopts "NF-IQL," which completely avoids sampling actions from the current policy and instead scales up the likelihood of actions already present in the offline dataset according to their advantages (action quality). This completely bypasses the sequential generation loop during training. In the inference phase, the trained AR-NF is distilled into a bidirectional one-step action generator that predicts all actions in parallel, removing the overhead of sequential inverse transformations.

Evaluated on simulated manipulation benchmarks (MetaWorld, LIBERO, RoboMimic) and real-world robots featuring bimanual setups and multi-fingered hands, RoMAN-Flow outperformed existing RL methods and VLA baselines. Furthermore, the one-step distillation cut inference latency by about 8.55x while maintaining competitive performance.
contributions: Proposed RoMAN-Flow, an autoregressive normalizing flow (AR-NF) policy framework for offline RL in robotic manipulation that combines exact continuous-action likelihood evaluation with high expressiveness.
Developed NF-IQL, which optimizes advantage-weighted exact likelihoods of dataset actions directly without sampling any actions from the current policy.
Established a one-step policy distillation method that eliminates the autoregressive sequential inverse process, accelerating inference by ~8.55x (to 81.5 ms) while maintaining task success rates.
Demonstrated superior performance over state-of-the-art diffusion and flow-matching baselines across MetaWorld, LIBERO, RoboMimic, and a real-world multi-fingered robot hand system.

sections.heading: Why Bring Normalizing Flows to Robot Control Now?
sections.summary: While diffusion and flow matching excel at generating actions, computing their exact likelihoods is expensive, hindering direct optimization in offline RL. This paper adopts Autoregressive Normalizing Flows (AR-NFs), which combine expressiveness with exact likelihood evaluation, and introduces a framework that overcomes their slow sampling speed.
sections.details:
In recent robotic manipulation, large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have gained massive attention. However, adapting them to real-world environments crucially relies on post-training via offline reinforcement learning (offline RL) using pre-collected datasets.

In the world of large language models (LLMs), autoregressive models can compute exact log-likelihoods, allowing likelihood-based post-training like DPO to work remarkably well. In robotics, however, mainstream approaches like Diffusion Policy and Flow Matching cannot cheaply compute exact conditional action likelihoods, making similar post-training difficult. Meanwhile, autoregressive policies using discrete action tokenization exist, but quantization can break continuous spatial geometry and temporal coordination.

This motivated the authors to explore Autoregressive Normalizing Flows (AR-NFs), which have achieved impressive results in areas like image generation. By pairing invertible mappings with an autoregressive structure, they can compute exact likelihoods directly on continuous actions. The catch is that AR-NFs have a fatal drawback: sampling via inverse transformation is sequential and very slow.

RoMAN-Flow overcomes this drawback in two stages. During policy optimization, it updates dataset action likelihoods using advantage weights without generating any policy samples. At deployment, it distills the policy into a one-step parallel generator. This delivers an approach that combines expressiveness, training efficiency, and inference speed.

sections.heading: Evolution of Generative Policies and Offline RL
sections.summary: Reinforcement learning for generative robot policies based on diffusion and flow matching has relied on surrogate losses and sample-based extraction due to intractable likelihoods. Normalizing flows provide exact density evaluation but historically lacked expressiveness; recent advances in AR-NFs make them a compelling alternative.
sections.details:
Related work can be organized along two main lines.

The first is the progress of generative policies in robot learning. To capture multimodal, complex action distributions, Diffusion Policy and Flow Matching (used in large VLAs like $\pi_0$) have become widespread. However, diffusion relies on denoising score matching, and continuous flows require numerical integration along generation ODEs, making it difficult to easily evaluate exact conditional action likelihoods. Consequently, applying RL has required complicated surrogate objectives.

The second is the lineage of offline RL and Normalizing Flows. In offline RL, advantage-weighted policy extraction (such as IQL) is widely used to prevent distribution shift where policies drift away from dataset actions and overestimate out-of-distribution values. Traditional normalizing flows (like RealNVP) offer exact density evaluation but lack the expressiveness needed for complex manipulation tasks.

Recently, AR-NFs such as SimFlow and TarFlow combined Transformers with autoregressive transformations, achieving both high expressiveness and exact likelihood computation. One-step distillation techniques like FARMER have also emerged. RoMAN-Flow synthesizes these insights into the first systematic framework tailored for continuous action-chunk control and offline RL in robotics.

sections.heading: How RoMAN-Flow Works: Sampling-Free RL and One-Step Distillation
sections.summary: RoMAN-Flow builds an AR-NF policy that invertibly maps continuous action chunks and initializes it with imitation learning. In offline RL (NF-IQL), it evaluates no samples from the policy, instead maximizing advantage-weighted likelihoods of offline actions in parallel, before distilling into a one-step student model.
sections.details:
The RoMAN-Flow pipeline consists of four key components: problem setup, AR-NF policy formulation, post-training via NF-IQL, and one-step distillation.

- Problem Formulation (3.1): Actions are modeled in chunks of length $H$, $\mathbf{a}_t = (a_t, \ldots, a_{t+H-1})$. The goal is to improve the policy using a reward-labeled offline dataset without additional environment interactions.

- Autoregressive Normalizing Flow Policy (3.2): Observations are encoded into context tokens $\mathbf{C}_t$ using a multimodal encoder such as a pretrained VLM. The AR-NF uses a SimFlow architecture, passing actions through $L$ invertible flow blocks. Inside each block, a Transformer with a causal attention mask predicts affine transformation parameters (shift $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and scale $\mathbf{s}$) at each action index $j$. Because the Jacobian is triangular, the log-likelihood $\log p_\theta(\mathbf{a}_t | \mathbf{C}_t)$ can be computed exactly and in parallel across all indices. Conversely, generating actions requires sequential inverse transformations.

- Post-Training with NF-IQL (3.3): This is the central design choice. Standard Actor-Critic methods sample actions from the policy to evaluate them with a critic, but doing so with AR-NFs leads to prohibitively slow training due to sequential generation. RoMAN-Flow adopts an IQL framework that evaluates only dataset actions. A Chunk Transformer Critic estimates Q-values for action prefixes, yielding an advantage $A_t$ against a state value $V$. Using weights $w_t = \exp(\beta A_t)$, it minimizes the weighted negative log-likelihood of offline actions. Because it requires only forward passes, training is sampling-free and remarkably fast.

- One-Step Policy Distillation (3.4): To eliminate deployment latency, the optimized AR-NF acts as a teacher and is distilled into a student model equipped with bidirectional attention. Using both offline actions perturbed with small noise and trajectories decoded by the teacher from prior latents, the student is trained via intermediate flow-state alignment and final action reconstruction losses. At inference, the student predicts the entire action chunk in a single parallel step.

captions.F2: Conceptual diagram of one-step policy distillation. The bidirectional Transformer student (One-step Actor) learns to match the intermediate flow states and final action chunks of the sequential autoregressive teacher (AR-NF Actor) in a single forward pass.

sections.heading: Simulated and Real-Robot Benchmarks: High Success and Low Latency
sections.summary: RoMAN-Flow was evaluated on MetaWorld-MT50, LIBERO, RoboMimic, and real-world bimanual/multi-fingered hand platforms. Offline RL produced significant gains over imitation learning, outperforming state-of-the-art VLA and diffusion models, while distillation cut inference latency by ~8.55x.
sections.details:
Extensive simulated and real-world experiments evaluated each phase: imitation learning (IL), post-reinforcement learning (NF-IQL), and post-distillation (One-Step).

- MetaWorld-MT50: Average success across 50 tasks improved substantially from 72.8% with IL to 81.1% with NF-IQL, with especially large leaps on Medium, Hard, and Very Hard splits. The distilled One-Step model retained 78.5%. Compared to $\pi_0$ + Flow-SDE (78.1%), which relies on online RL, fully offline RoMAN-Flow (NF-IQL) was 3.0 percentage points higher.

- LIBERO: Across four suites, average success rose from 93.5% (IL) to 95.3% (NF-IQL). In particular, LIBERO-Long saw a 6.6-point improvement. The One-Step model maintained 93.7%, slightly surpassing the teacher on LIBERO-Long at 93.0%.

- RoboMimic MH: Comparing against prior work SERNF (RealNVP + TD3+BC) on the Square task, SERNF scored 68% while RoMAN-Flow (NF-IQL) reached 85%, and the One-Step variant remained strong at 80%.

- Real-Robot Experiments: Using a 7-DoF Franka arm and a 12-DoF XHand multi-fingered hand, pick-and-place tasks with beakers and cylinders were evaluated. In out-of-distribution (OOD) setups where objects were placed in unvisited regions, average success jumped 24.2 percentage points from 57.3% (IL) to 81.5% (NF-IQL), beating the $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline (71.8%).

- Inference Speed and Model Scaling: On LIBERO-Long, generation latency dropped from ~697 ms with the AR-NF teacher to 81.5 ms with the one-step student, achieving an ~8.55x speedup. In actor scaling ablations, performance remained flat when expanding from 33.8M to 466.2M parameters, but scaling up to 685.5M (XL) produced a notable jump to 85% success on Square.

captions.F3: Rollouts of RoMAN-Flow across MetaWorld, LIBERO-Long, RoboMimic, and physical robots. Bottom right: Franka arm with a 12-DoF XHand successfully executes high-precision grasping and scale-placement of an out-of-distribution beaker.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: RoMAN-Flow makes exact likelihood-based offline reinforcement learning practical for robotic manipulation by using autoregressive normalizing flows. Its sampling-free training algorithm and one-step distillation successfully unite high performance with real-time speed.
sections.details:
This paper introduced RoMAN-Flow, an offline reinforcement learning framework that leverages Autoregressive Normalizing Flows (AR-NFs) as robotic manipulation policies.

To tackle the primary bottleneck of AR-NFs—slow sequential sampling—the authors provided clean solutions: NF-IQL removes policy sampling during post-training, and one-step distillation converts the model into a fast bidirectional generator for deployment. Across simulation and real-world experiments, the framework proved to be a powerful and practical alternative to diffusion and flow-matching policies.

Establishing a continuous policy family that supports exact likelihood evaluation opens the door for alignment and post-training techniques developed in the LLM community to translate more directly into robotics.

sections.heading: Appendix: Reward Relabeling Tricks and Implementation Details
sections.summary: To improve credit assignment under sparse rewards, the authors introduced adaptive reward relabeling based on Monte Carlo return ranks. The appendix also provides observation setups and hyperparameter details across benchmarks.
sections.details:
Several key implementation details are highlighted to better understand the paper:

- Reward Relabeling (6.2): Robotic manipulation often features sparse rewards given only at task completion, complicating TD credit assignment. Inspired by HUBL, the authors introduced an adaptive relabeling scheme that interpolates between observed future returns and bootstrapped value estimates using a weight $\lambda_n$ based on the trajectory's average Monte Carlo return rank. Trajectories with higher ranks trust the empirical future returns more heavily.

- Backbone Architecture (7.1): For LIBERO, MetaWorld, and real-robot setups, SmolVLM-500M-Instruct serves as the multimodal encoder, processing images, language instructions, and proprioceptive states (joint positions) uniformly. For RoboMimic, dual ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 encoders (agent-view and eye-in-hand cameras) are used for fair comparison with SERNF.

- Parameter Count and Distillation Efficiency (7.1): The SmolVLM-based AR-NF policy has around 1.45B parameters, while the distilled one-step student has about 0.56B parameters, cutting the model size by more than half. In RoboMimic, the actor portion is compressed from 0.95B down to 78.2M.

captions.F6: Representative successful rollouts across the LIBERO benchmark suites. The policy reliably executes multi-step sequences across spatial layout changes (Spatial), object variations (Object), language goals (Goal), and extended horizons (Long).

takeaways: AR-NFs can compute exact log-likelihoods in continuous action spaces, making them exceptionally well suited for likelihood-based RL (such as DPO and IQL) in robotics.

The slow generation speed of autoregressive models can be fully bypassed through a two-stage approach: sampling-free objectives (IQL) during training, followed by one-step distillation for deployment.
As demonstrated by model scaling ablations, scaling actor capacity up to ~0.7B parameters is critical for tackling contact-rich, high-precision tasks like Square.
limitations: While one-step distillation preserves most performance, a few tasks (e.g., in MetaWorld and RoboMimic) still show a minor drop of a few percentage points compared to the teacher model.
Because the offline RL phase relies entirely on actions present in the dataset, performance improvements can plateau if the dataset contains no high-quality trajectories or clues for improvement.
Maximizing the expressiveness of the AR-NF actor requires relatively large parameter counts (hundreds of millions to over 1B), leading to significant GPU memory usage during training.
